A contrail is a long, white, cloud-like streak that forms in the sky directly behind a flying aircraft — most commonly a jet plane at high altitude. It is essentially a man-made cloud, triggered by the plane's engines.
What is actually happening when a contrail forms?

When a jet engine burns fuel, it releases hot exhaust gases. These gases contain a significant amount of water vapor — the same invisible gas that makes up humidity in the air around you.

Now, high up in the atmosphere where commercial planes fly (roughly 8 to 12 kilometers above the ground), the air is brutally cold — often around −40°C or even colder. When the hot, moisture-laden exhaust shoots out of the engine and instantly hits this freezing air, the water vapor has no choice but to condense and freeze almost immediately. It turns into millions of tiny ice crystals.

These tiny ice crystals are what you see. Just like any cloud is made of tiny water droplets or ice crystals that scatter sunlight, a contrail is the same thing — except it was created by a plane, not by natural atmospheric processes. This is why contrails are also called vapor trails or condensation trails.

A helpful analogy: You have almost certainly seen your own breath on a cold winter morning. That puff of white mist happens because warm, moist air from your lungs hits the cold outside air and the water vapor condenses into tiny droplets — making it briefly visible. A contrail is exactly the same principle, just happening at extreme altitude and on a much larger, longer scale.
What does a contrail look like?

A fresh contrail appears as a sharp, thin, bright-white line slicing across the blue sky, trailing directly behind the plane. As time passes, it may stay thin and crisp, or it may slowly spread outward and become a wider, hazier, wispy band that looks remarkably like a natural high-altitude cloud. In heavily trafficked flight corridors, you can sometimes see multiple contrails running parallel to each other or crossing, forming grid-like patterns across the sky.
Why do some contrails disappear quickly while others last for hours?

This is one of the most interesting things about contrails: their lifespan depends entirely on the moisture content of the surrounding air.

  • If the air at that altitude is dry, the ice crystals evaporate back into invisible water vapor within seconds to a couple of minutes. The contrail appears and vanishes quickly.
  • If the air is already very humid (close to saturation), the ice crystals have nowhere to evaporate into. They persist, spread laterally due to upper-atmosphere winds, and can linger for many hours — sometimes covering large portions of the sky in a thin, milky haze.

So when you notice that a contrail lingers and spreads for a long time, it is actually telling you something true about the atmospheric conditions at that altitude: the air up there is quite moist.

At lower altitudes, where the air is warmer, the exhaust does not cool fast enough to produce visible ice crystals. Most contrails form above roughly 8,000 meters, where temperatures are sufficiently low. A plane flying at a lower altitude on a warm day may leave no visible trail at all.
Are there different types of contrails?

Yes, two main types:

  1. Engine contrails — by far the most common. These form directly from the hot, moist exhaust coming out of jet engines, exactly as described above.
  2. Aerodynamic contrails — these are rarer and form through a completely different mechanism. When a wing (or propeller) slices through air, it causes a rapid drop in air pressure right around the wing tip. A sudden drop in pressure causes a sudden drop in temperature. If the air is moist enough, this brief local cooling can condense the water vapor into a thin streak of cloud. You sometimes see these as short wisps curling off the tips of wings during certain weather conditions, or on a commercial plane during landing when the flaps are deployed.
Do contrails have any effect on the environment?

Yes, and this is an important and actively studied area of science. Contrails are not merely decorative — they behave like artificial cirrus clouds (the thin, wispy, high-altitude clouds), and like all clouds, they interact with the Earth's energy balance:

  • Warming effect: Contrails trap heat radiating upward from the Earth's surface (just like a blanket), which tends to warm the atmosphere slightly. This effect is stronger at night when there is no sunlight to reflect.
  • Cooling effect: Contrails also reflect some incoming sunlight back into space, which has a slight cooling effect.
  • The net effect of persistent contrails is generally considered to be a mild warming influence, and their combined impact on climate from global aviation is considered significant enough that researchers are exploring ways to reduce it — for example, by slightly adjusting flight altitudes to avoid the most humidity-saturated atmospheric layers.

Some people claim that persistent, spreading contrails are actually "chemtrails" — chemicals secretly sprayed from planes for various alleged purposes. This idea is not supported by any scientific evidence. Contrails are a completely understood atmospheric phenomenon. Their persistence and spreading behavior are explained by well-established atmospheric physics, and the variation in how long they last matches exactly what meteorologists would predict based on measured humidity at altitude. Scientists, independent pilots, atmospheric chemists, and aviation engineers across the world have studied this thoroughly, and there is no credible evidence for anything beyond ordinary ice crystal formation.

A contrail is a long, white, cloud-like streak formed in the sky behind a jet aircraft when the hot, moisture-containing exhaust from its engines freezes instantly upon contact with the extremely cold air at high altitude, creating a trail of tiny ice crystals that is, in every meaningful sense, a man-made cloud.
